attempts.evidence: the threshold fell to en 13.74 / ru 3.78 and the corpus reported no false conversion on every population, but driving the engine showed that of the nineteen Russian sequences newly converted exactly one was genuine wrong-layout text: `гифка`->`ubarf`, `Ютуб`->`Юne,`, `флуд`->`akel`, `какбэ`->`rfr,'`, `тыща`->`nsof` are ordinary Russian. The filter removed the hard negatives rather than the untrustworthy labels. Found by the fourth pre-release review.
attempts.idea: discount a negative label the corpus cannot stand behind: the sentence around it is not verifiably monolingual, the snapshot shows the token once, or the token reads as an ordinary word of the other language
attempts.result: corrupts ordinary words; the measured safety was hollow

description: Six ways of separating the residual class - foreign words, names and garbage that no dictionary knows - from text genuinely typed in the wrong layout. Each was measured and each cost more accuracy than it bought. They are kept so the next attempt starts where this one stopped.
lesson: Excluding a label does not make the token safe to convert; it only hides it from the metric. The negative population must hold every token the engine can present, whatever one thinks of its label. A wrong label costs recall; excluding a real word costs the user's text.
what_would_help: A corpus whose language label is verified per token rather than inherited from the sentence. Tatoeba cannot give that: its Russian sentences contain English typed in the wrong layout - `пдфку` is `glare` - and those tokens are labelled Russian, so they demand that the model leave alone exactly what it exists to convert.
why_the_class_exists: The tokens this model must convert are, by construction, not ordinary words of the target language: they are commands, abbreviations and technical terms. Any hypothesis that captures 'this is not an ordinary word' captures them too.
